title: Orthogonal Benchmarking Protocol and Regression Runbook
body:
Purpose and scope:
This doc defines an orthogonal benchmark protocol and accompanying regression runbook intended to isolate performance regressions across three primary runtime subsystems: kernel execution (low-level operator/kernels), request scheduling & batching, and the KV cache (prefix/KV reuse and cache churn). The goal is to make regressions reproducible, attributable, and actionable with a small, repeatable matrix of microbenchmarks + seeded traces. This is deliberately distinct from prior trace-synthesis and probe playbooks — it prioritizes orthogonality (one variable at a time), compact experiment vectors, and an explicit triage decision tree.

Goals:
- Provide a short, runnable protocol to isolate whether a perf regression is kernel, scheduler, or kv-cache related within 1–2 hours of investigation.
- Produce minimal synthetic workloads and trace seeds that exercise orthogonal axes: sequence length distribution, cache hit ratio, concurrency/batching patterns, and KV churn.
- Define detection thresholds and statistical checks to avoid noisy false-positive regressions.
- Supply a step-by-step triage runbook mapping signals to likely root causes and quick repro/mitigation steps.

High-level approach (orthogonalization):
We define 4 axes and build microbenchmarks that vary a single axis while holding the others constant. For each run we collect a standard metric set (latency percentiles, tokens/sec, GPU SM util, host CPU, scheduler queue depth, KV cache hit ratio, memory alloc stats, kernel selection logs).
Axes:
- A: Sequence length distribution (short: <32, medium: 128, long: 1024)
- B: KV cache hit ratio (0%, 25%, 75%, 95%)
- C: Batch size / request concurrency (1, 4, 16, 64 effective requests)
- D: KV churn pattern (steady reuse, rotating prefixes, cold-start bursts)

Experiment matrix (minimal):
- Core microbench suite (16 runs): combine A=short/long with B=0%/95% and C=1/16 to cover extremes. These runs quickly surface either kernel-level tail (long seq), batcher inefficiencies (high C with small tokens), or caching issues (different B).
- Churn sweep (8 runs): keep A=medium, C=4, vary D across predefined rotation sets to stress cache garbage/eviction paths.
- Concurrency sweep (8 runs): keep A=short, B=95%, vary C to exercise scheduler and batching thresholds.
- Smoke trace replays (3 traces): replay 3 curated mini-traces from production: very-chatty (many short requests), long-context (document summarization flows), and mixed (moderate long + short). These verify that microbench signals hold under realistic scheduling noise.

Instrumentation (must collect every run):
- Runtime metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec, requests/sec, per-request token counts.
- Kernel-level: kernel name fingerprint, kernel runtime histogram, number of kernel launches, effective batching per kernel call, kernel-specific memory copies.
- GPU counters: SM_util, achieved_occupancy, l2_bandwidth, memory_usage, cupti metrics (if available).
- Host: CPU user/sys, queue length for scheduler queues, epoll wakeups/sec, network retransmits.
- KV cache: hit ratio, evictions/sec, cache size (entries & bytes), average prefix length, cache admission latency, per-request kv lookups.
- Trace pairing: record full request->kernel mapping (trace id), KV cache decision log (hit/miss/revoked), and scheduling timestamp chain (enqueue->dispatch->complete).

Runbook: how to execute the minimal diagnosis (approx 45–90 minutes)
1) Reproduce baseline: run the Core microbench suite on the failing commit and on the last-known-good commit. Use identical hardware and pinned models. Collect artifacts: perf tarball, trace logs, benchmark CSVs.
2) Quick delta check (10–15m): compute p95 delta and tokens/sec delta per run. If deltas < 5% across all runs, mark as noise. If one of the Core runs shows >15% regressive delta at p95 or >10% token/sec drop, continue.
3) Axis isolation:
   - If regressions only occur in long-sequence runs (A=long) but not short: suspect kernel-level algorithmic regression (attention, kv handling inside kernel, memory fragmentation).
   - If regressions magnify with concurrency (higher C): suspect scheduler/batcher changes (batch packing, queue head-of-line blocking, or lock contention).
   - If regressions correlate with low KV hit ratio (low B) but not high-B runs: suspect KV admission/exclusion path or eviction thrashing.
4) Confirm with micro-probes: enable kernel-level microbench (single kernel hotpath replay) and KV cache debug counters. For scheduler suspicion, run the Concurrency sweep with detailed scheduler traces.
5) Triage mapping (signals -> likely subsystems):
   - Kernel slowdowns: increased per-kernel runtime across many kernels; GPU SM_util unchanged or slightly higher; l2 bandwidth saturation; kernel selection changed to fallback variant.
   - Batcher/scheduler: increased queue depth, host CPU spikes in scheduler thread, decreased effective batching efficiency (more small kernel launches), wallclock latency rises with concurrency.
   - KV cache: hit ratio drops, eviction rate spikes, memory churn on host, latency spikes localized to requests that miss the cache and require full KV reconstruction.
6) Quick mitigations:
   - Kernel: roll back kernel selector changes, pin older kernel binary, or reduce sequence length as temporary guardrail.
   - Scheduler: reduce configured max concurrency, adjust packing window size, or revert last batching heuristics.
   - KV cache: increase cache size temporarily, lower eviction aggressiveness, or enable degraded LRU fallback.

Statistical checks and thresholds (recommended defaults):
- Use paired-run comparisons with bootstrapped p95 confidence intervals over 30–120 runs per microbench.
- Flag regression if p95 difference >= 15% AND absolute p95 increase >= 30ms for short-seq or >= 200ms for long-seq workloads.
- Token/sec drop flagged at >= 10% with p-value < 0.01 via bootstrap resampling.
- For flaky signals, require reproducibility across repeated runs separated by 10 minutes and across at least 2 identical machines.

Instrumentation recipes (commands and snippets):
- Microbench harness: scripts/bench/run_microbench.sh --profile=orthogonal --seq=long --kv-hit=0.95 --concurrency=16 --samples=50
- Trace replay: tools/trace/replay --seed traces/orthogonal/long-doc.json --preserve-timestamps --out /tmp/replay-logs
- Kernel probe: use /opt/serving/bin/kernel_probe --pid $PID --out kernel-profile.json (or CUPTI-based capture for detailed GPU metrics).
- NV counters: ncu --target-processes all --set full --output ncu-run ./serving-runtime --bench-config ...

Artifact collection checklist (for attaching to incident):
- benchmark CSVs for all runs (include config headers)
- kernel-profile.json and ncu/nvprof tarballs
- GPU usage logs and sysstat (iostat, vmstat) slices around test window
- trace replay logs and the original trace seeds
- config and commit hash + docker image id used
- minimal repro script to rerun the failing microbench

Known oddities & gotchas (learned):
- Small-seq p99 can be dominated by tail jitter from host GC or background cron jobs — prefer p95 for first-pass gating.
- High B (KV hit) runs can mask scheduler regressions because fewer kernel launches hide batching inefficiencies. Always run at least one low-B run.
- Kernel selector fallbacks show up as bimodal kernel runtime histograms; check kernel fingerprint logs for mixed variants.
- Trace replays that naively preserve timestamps can overwhelm the scheduler; use target RPS throttles to avoid adding noise.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Automate orthogonal microbench orchestration in CI with golden thresholds per model family. (JIRA-2187)
- Gather baseline golden profiles for top-10 customers' traces to expand the smoke set. (owner: Evan)
- Add a lightweight latency attribution UI in Console to show kernel vs scheduling vs cache contribution per request.

Appendix: diagnostic decision table (short):
- High p95 only on long-seq runs -> kernel path (attention, kv memcpy)
- High p95 which scales linearly with concurrency -> scheduler/batcher
- Localized high latency to requests with cache miss flag -> kv-cache eviction/rehydration
- Drop in tokens/sec with no p95 rise but increased GPU memcpy -> kernel IO-bound change
